title: Curated Clarity Closet
subtitle: A 30-day plan to wear, care for, and replace clothes in a compact home — without a magic body type
tagline: The care label wins. A capsule is not a number.
author: Akarsh Priyadarshan
closing_blurb: More room kits and measured layouts — same series language, same clear numbers. This book helps readers run a 30-day closet plan they can actually maintain. It does not diagnose undertone, replace a care label, or guarantee a capsule size.

chapters.title: Days 1–3: Clarify how you live
chapters.intro: How to use this book: it is a 30-day guided closet plan, not a set of modules that each restart at Day 1. Follow Days 1–30 in order, or pause a phase if life interrupts — then resume at the next unfinished day. This book is for people building practical wardrobes in compact homes and everyday urban environments. Examples use different cities and lifestyles for illustration; adapt quantities, fabrics, care, and budgets to your climate, culture, work, and storage. Some scenarios use Indian cities as compact-home illustrations. They do not define the market. Prices are USD. Measurements, when given, are inches and are illustrations. Manufacturer care labels, the lease, and a qualified cleaner or cobbler take precedence. A capsule is a working group of clothes you actually wear, not a fixed number and not a ban on uniforms, sportswear, sleepwear, occasionwear, cultural clothing, or sentimental pieces. First-use meanings: Style North Star — a short description of how you want clothes to work for your real week. Outfit equation — a repeatable formula such as bottom plus top plus layer. Micro capsule — a small working subset for one context, not a mandatory item count. Archetype — a pattern you already wear, optional, not a personality test. Acquisition ratio — a planning mix of core versus accent buys, not a law. Cost per wear — purchase price divided by wears so far, a comparison aid. Fit Fabric Function Score — a 1–5 decision aid, not a lab measurement. Wear log — a record of what you actually put on. Silhouette grid — notes on shapes that move with your day, not an ideal body. Do not use load-bearing walls or other apartment structure notes unless they change hanging or storage. Use hanging space, shared wardrobes, laundry access, commute, and time instead.

sections.scenario: Sensory sensitivity: a 'perfect' silhouette scored high and still itched all day.
sections.principle: Equal weight 1–5. A veto beats a high total.
body: Today's output: score only borderline items. Five criteria, equal weight, each 1 to 5. 1 means unusable for that criterion. 5 means it works for your real week without extra effort. There is no minimum total that forces Keep. Add the five numbers if you want a snapshot. The snapshot is a personal decision aid, not an objective measure of quality or attractiveness.

If an item scores well overall but causes discomfort, pain, instability, or a care method you cannot do, that is a veto. Put it in Tailor, Test, or Exit. A serious comfort, safety, or care problem remains a veto even when the overall score is high.
Suggested use, not a law: totals that still have a veto never Keep; mixed scores with no veto go to Test; high totals with no veto may Keep if you will actually wear them.

body: Today's output: each Exit item routed. Good condition and clean: donate, resell, or gift. Needs minor repair: repair before release. Damaged but usable as textile: local recycling or repurpose if those exist. Wet, moldy, contaminated, or pest-affected: isolate; clean or dispose using appropriate local guidance — do not donate. Memory: photograph, limited physical keep, review date.

Do not dump contaminated textiles on a charity. Do not force a same-day decision on every sentimental piece. If you use a textile collection or recycling drop-off, verify that service actually accepts this material — fiber mix, shoes, and wet or moldy items are often refused. A city without that service is normal; then dispose of unusable items using ordinary household rules, not a pretend recycle.

chapters.intro: Care-label-first. Heat and steam are not automatically safe. Cedar is not the same as a pesticide moth product. Store only what is fully dry.

sections.title: The care label wins

hero.query: A close-up of a well-organized closet section with color-coded clothing and labeled containers, emphasizing visibility and accessibility.

sections.scenario: Unknown finish: a coated jacket and a steamer.
sections.principle: If the label is missing or fights this book, go gentler or ask a cleaner.
body: Today's output: the care-label-first rule written where you do laundry. Follow the label when it is clear. Dry clean only: do not experiment at home. Unknown fabric or finish: test cautiously or get professional advice. Mold, persistent odor, or pests: isolate and choose an appropriate method. Heat-sensitive: do not assume steam or ironing is safe. Heat can harm coatings, prints, elastics, and glued details. Test an unfamiliar detergent on a hidden seam. Cedar blocks are not the same as moth-repellent pesticides — read those product labels and keep chemicals away from children and pets as directed.
Never store a garment until it is fully dry. Closed closets plus damp clothes are a mold problem.

body: Today's output: a Laundry Flow — 1 clean and ready; 2 worn once and OK to air and re-wear; 3 laundry required; 4 repair or stain treatment; 5 seasonal storage. Frequency depends on garment, body contact, activity, climate, odor, and the care label.

Odor, sweat, or a stain: do not return to the ready rail. Limited drying space: wash smaller loads; use ventilation the lease allows; do not trap damp items. Humid or monsoon conditions: extra dry time before hanging in the closet.

sections.scenario: Rainy-season commute: wet sneakers in a closed wardrobe.
sections.principle: No single capsule mix fits every climate.
body: Today's output: climate notes plus a completed footwear-care checklist. Do not use one cleaning method for leather, suede, fabric, and synthetics. Follow the manufacturer for that pair.

Footwear-care checklist: dry wet shoes before storage; rotate frequently worn pairs so they can air; clean leather, suede, fabric, and synthetic materials each according to that product's instructions; check sole wear, grip, and structural damage; separate pairs that need repair from pairs ready to wear; do not use damaged footwear when it creates a safety or comfort issue.

Accessories and shoes schedule, adapted to use and the maker: after use — air and remove visible dirt where appropriate; weekly or as needed — inspect frequently used footwear and accessories; monthly — check damage, loose hardware, sole wear, and repair needs; seasonally — review what was stored or exposed to rain, humidity, or dust. Seasonal garment storage remains: clean and fully dry, repair first, breathable storage if appropriate, do not overpack, label, inspect before re-entry.
